title: Back-Rank Mate
subtitle: When the king's own pawns become its prison
summary: Unmoved kingside pawns can trap a king on the back rank. This study shows the deflection that removes the only defender and the mate that follows.

rootAnnotations.title: The pawn shield becomes a prison
rootAnnotations.body: Black's f7, g7, and h7 pawns are still on their starting squares. They look like protection, but they also block every escape square along the king's own rank — g7 and h7 belong to the pawns, and f8/h8 are only safe if nothing attacks them. A rook or queen that reaches the back rank uncontested delivers mate on the spot.

rootAnnotations.title: One weak move is enough
rootAnnotations.body: Black's rook on f8 is currently the only piece guarding the back rank. Overload it, deflect it, or remove it, and the whole rank collapses. That is the entire back-rank lesson in one sentence.

annotations.title: Lining up the shot
annotations.body: The queen steps onto the a3-f8 diagonal, attacking the rook on f8 — Black's only defender of the back rank. Nothing recaptures on f8 except the king, and the king can't reach it in time.

annotations.title: A quiet move that ignores the real danger
annotations.body: This looks harmless, but Black needed to deal with the threat against f8 right now — by moving the rook, or defending it. A move like this is exactly how back-rank disasters happen in real games: nothing looks urgent until it's too late.

annotations.title: Deflecting the only defender
annotations.body: The queen gives itself up for the rook, but that's not the point — capturing on f8 is check, and it strips away the one piece guarding the back rank. Kxf8 is forced; nothing else can answer the check.

annotations.title: Forced
annotations.body: The king has no alternative — nothing else can capture on f8 or block the check, so this is the only legal reply.

annotations.title: The mating point
annotations.body: The rook on e8 is defended by the bishop on a4 along the a4-e8 diagonal, so Kxe8 is illegal. The king's other squares are all covered: e7 and g8 are attacked by the rook along the rank, and f7/g7 are blocked by Black's own pawns. That's checkmate.

annotations.title: Luft would have saved Black
annotations.body: A single move like ...h6 earlier in the game — creating 'luft', or breathing room, for the king — would have given the king an escape square on h7 and defused this entire combination. Making luft before it's needed is one of the most useful habits in chess.
